segments.title: Introduction to Big O Notation in Computer Science

sub_topics.name: Introduction
sub_topics.description: Hey, what's going on everybody? It's your bro, hope you're doing well, and in this video I'm going to describe the very basics of Big O notation in, well, computer science.

sub_topics.name: Definition of Big O Notation
sub_topics.description: Oh yeah, Big O notation. So a common phrase used with Big O notation is, how code slows as data grows. It describes the performance of an algorithm as the amount of data increases.

key_points: Big O notation is used to describe the performance of an algorithm
It describes how code slows as data grows

segments.title: Examples of Big O Notation in Computer Science

sub_topics.name: Example 1: Addup Function
sub_topics.description: Here's a more concrete example. I have a function named addup. We will add up to a certain number depending on what we pass in as an argument.

sub_topics.name: Example 2: Optimized Addup Function
sub_topics.description: Now another way which we could write the same function is to take sum equals n times n plus 1 divided by 2. We will get the exact same sum.

key_points: Big O notation can be used to compare the performance of different algorithms
Optimized algorithms can significantly improve performance

segments.title: Runtime Complexities in Big O Notation

sub_topics.name: Constant Time
sub_topics.description: Anything that has a runtime complexity of O of 1 will take the same amount of time regardless of the data size.

sub_topics.name: Logarithmic Time
sub_topics.description: One example is binary search. Anything that has a runtime complexity of O of log n will actually take, I don't want to say less and less time, but increasingly less time to complete.

sub_topics.name: Linear Time
sub_topics.description: As the amount of data increases, the time it takes to complete something will increase proportionally linearly. That would include looping through the elements in an array and searching through a linked list.

sub_topics.name: Quasi-Linear Time
sub_topics.description: This would include a quick sort, merge sort, and heap sort. We'll talk about these concepts in future videos.

sub_topics.name: Quadratic Time
sub_topics.description: As the amount of data increases, it's going to take increasingly more and more time to complete anything that has a runtime complexity of O of n squared.

sub_topics.name: Factorial Time
sub_topics.description: One place where this is used is with the traveling salesman problem, which I might discuss in a future video. So this is extremely slow, so if I had to give a letter grade to each of these runtime complexities when working with large data sets with constant time, this would be an A, like an A+.

sub_topics.name: Conclusion
sub_topics.description: Well, that's the very basics of Big O notation. It's notation used to describe the performance of an algorithm as the amount of data increases.

key_points: There are different types of runtime complexities in Big O notation
Each type has its own characteristics and use cases
